1.pericope_label: Judge me, O Lord; for I have walked in mine integrity... For thy lovingkindness is before mine eyes: and I have walked in thy truth

schools.summary: Renders the opening plea as do me justice, vindicate me, and corrects the received sense of the following clause to I have trusted without wavering; on the request to be tried it argues that the verb should on the right reading be purify, the Greek having tried by fire. A second voice places the psalm beside its predecessor and makes the sharpest observation in the chapter: the two are bound together at several points, yet this one lacks entirely the self-accusation that there accompanies the attestation of piety, the harshness of the contrast with these enemies leaving no room for such a lament. It also defines the two nouns of the third verse as divine love condescending to sinners and the truth by which God adheres to that love and to his promise.

Distinguishes the two justifications: this is not the justification of the psalmist's person, which he knew was not by his own righteousness, but of his cause before men. Supplies the figure of gold tried by the touchstone for the examination asked, and traces the lovingkindness pleaded back through the choice of him in Christ to a love from everlasting. A second voice notes that the verb denotes the act of a judge and of an advocate alike and prefers the advocate sense as agreeing with the psalm's scope, drawing the lesson that when God leaves us to our enemies he seems to neglect our cause, but when he restrains them our defence is shown to be his care.

Reasons from the sheer number of protestations that the psalm is a vindication against alleged plots, and reports without adopting a suggestion that it and the two after it form one ode from the captivity. Makes the denial specific — the psalmist never plotted against any man's life or property, nor coveted the crown — and welcomes the examination, wishing every motive of his heart dissected and exposed to God's view. A second voice makes the sense of lovingkindness the reason he dares appeal at all.

Sets the psalm under Saul's persecution, when the enemies dressed the psalmist in the skins of wild beasts to bait him, and observes that innocency is no fence to the name, though it is to the bosom, against the darts of calumny. States the limit as doctrine: David cannot justify himself against the charge of sin, but he can against the charge of hypocrisy. Warns that the appeal should not be borrowed carelessly, since a man had need have a clear case who dares carry his suit into the King's Bench of heaven — though where conscience approves, the comfort is great.

Builds the qualification into the plea itself, allowing some desert of innocence only after the mercy God first showed, and trusting not in himself but in the Lord. On the request to be tried he asks that the proving make him known not to God, from whom nothing is hid, but to himself and to men, and that the burning of the reins be a remedial purgation applied to his thoughts.

positions.summary: The persecution under Saul, the psalmist answering false accusations at court.
The Absalom conspiracy, whose hypocritical leaders the description fits.
Some contest with hypocrites that cannot be dated; the particular events are not indicated.

debates.question: How can so strong a protestation of innocence be made to God?

positions.summary: By distinguishing the charges: not innocence of sin, which is confessed, but innocence of the hypocrisy alleged.
Only within limits, and never of one's whole walk except as justified in Christ.
By grounding it in prior mercy: any desert of innocence follows the mercy God first showed, and it is his mercy, not merit, that stands before the eyes.
It is simply absent here, and its absence is itself the psalm's distinguishing feature against the psalm before it.

outliers.reading: Assigns the psalm neither to David alone nor to Christ the Mediator, but to the whole Church now perfectly established in him.

themes: Judge me, O Lord; for I have walked in mine integrity: I have trusted also in the Lord; therefore I shall not slide.
Examine me, O Lord, and prove me; try my reins and my heart.
For thy lovingkindness is before mine eyes: and I have walked in thy truth.

4.pericope_label: I have not sat with vain persons, neither will I go in with dissemblers... That I may publish with the voice of thanksgiving, and tell of all thy wondrous works

schools.summary: Presses the vocabulary of the company avoided: the word for vain persons carries the chaotic void of alienation from God and untruth whitewashed over with dissimulation, while the second class are the veiled, who keep their mischievous designs secret. The word behind evildoers carries the idea of violence, from a root meaning to break in pieces. On the washing it distinguishes a symbolic action from the figure of speech it later became, prefers that I may to so will I, and doubts the circling of the altar, no other reference to the practice occurring in Jewish literature. A second voice holds that the symbolic act appears here only as a figure of innocence, the whole petition resting on love for a sanctuary now far off.

Catalogues the vain persons as men addicted to the world's vanities, unruly talkers and idolaters, and adds the distinction that what the psalmist hated was their works and not their persons. Hears in the washing the priests' preparation and also the lifting up of holy hands in prayer, and observes at the close that what was to be offered on the altar so compassed was not a slain beast but the sacrifice of praise.

Reads the whole passage politically: men of lies and backbiters, then the hidden ones and secret plotters in the state, then crowds of discontented men who under pretence of reform strove to subvert it. Supplies the historical practice behind the washing, which sometimes declared innocence of a base transaction, and notes that walking round a superior or a temple is a mark of respect elsewhere in the world. A second voice reduces the verse to an impossibility: he could not approach the altar with any comfort if conscious of the crimes alleged.

Turns the avoidance into evidence — a man is known by his company, and he who was never in the parish is not likely to have stolen the corn — while conceding that we must see and trade with men of the world and insisting only that we not take our rest in their empty society. Treats the washing as real preparation, habitual and actual, with the psalmist looking to the substance of what the priests were enjoined in shadow, and is careful about how much innocence is claimed: not perfection, but freedom from the crimes charged.

debates.question: Are the washing and the circling of the altar acts performed or figures of speech?

positions.summary: A figure only: what is elsewhere a symbolic act is here rhetoric confessing consciousness of innocence.
First a symbolic action, later a figure of speech — and the circling itself is doubtful, since no other Jewish source describes it.
Real preparation for worship, habitual and actual, taking the substance of what the priests had in shadow.

debates.question: Who are the vain persons and dissemblers?

positions.summary: Unreality itself given human form — hollowness of disposition and alienation from God, masked by hypocrisy.
Political actors: liars, backbiters, and the secret plotters and conspirators of the state.
A broad moral class — the worldly, the empty talker, the idolater — to be shunned in every form.

outliers.reading: Infers from the comparison of the washing with the command about the laver that the psalm is Levitical in authorship, or at least in character — a conclusion about who wrote it drawn from a single ritual allusion.

themes: I have not sat with vain persons, neither will I go in with dissemblers.
I have hated the congregation of evil doers; and will not sit with the wicked.
I will wash mine hands in innocency: so will I compass thine altar, O Lord:
That I may publish with the voice of thanksgiving, and tell of all thy wondrous works.

8.pericope_label: Lord, I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place where thine honour dwelleth... My foot standeth in an even place: in the congregations will I bless the Lord

schools.summary: Reads the closing petition as a prayer to be spared while doom falls on the evildoers, noting that the Greek and Latin render it destroy not; and alone among the voices it takes the final verse as a condition rather than a report — when I stand in an even place, that is, when I am rescued, then I will praise. A second voice calls that verse the epilogue, in which prayer changes into rejoicing certain of its answer: hitherto shut in as though in trackless gorges, the psalmist now stands on a plain commanding a wide range of vision and blends his praise with the congregation's song.

Dates the sanctuary reference, since the temple was not yet built. Allows the closing petition both senses, that he might not be brought into such company or destroyed with it, and observes that death is regularly described as a gathering to one's people; distinguishes mischief contrived from mischief committed; turns the walking in integrity forward to what follows death; and locates the even place on Christ as the sure foundation.

Translates the eighth verse as the habitation of thy house and the place of the tabernacle of thy glory, identifying the holy of holies and the mercy seat and deriving from the word for dwelling the familiar name of the manifested presence. Reads the petition of the final lot, identifies the men of the tenth verse as officials who took bribes, and lists what the settled standing rests on — abhorring evil, avoiding the wicked, frequenting the ordinances, and depending on mercy alone. A second voice glosses the house as sanctuary and worship and takes the ground as already sure.

Gives the closing petition its most concrete form — when, like fruit, I must be gathered, put me not in the same basket with the best of sinners — and grounds it in the psalm's earlier separation. On the protest against unrighteous gain it makes the psalmist a nonconformist swimming like a live fish against the stream, while insisting he is no boaster, since integrity is a work of grace marred by infirmity and saints must still bow as sinners. Hears the last verse as a modulation from minor to major, and closes in company: let us not forsake the assembling of ourselves together, and let the slanderers howl outside the door while the children sing within.

debates.question: What does gather not my soul with sinners ask for?

positions.summary: Preservation now, while judgment sweeps the evildoers away — the versions read destroy not.
A different eternal lot: not to be bound up in the same bundle with them.
Either, and both at once — not to be brought into their company in life, and not to be destroyed with them at the end.

debates.question: Does the last verse report a rescue or await one?

positions.summary: Reports it: the ground is already firm, the prayer already turned to rejoicing certain of its answer.
Awaits it: the drift of the poem favours reading a condition — when I am rescued from these difficulties, then I will praise.

outliers.reading: Uses the verse's word for dwelling to explain the origin of the traditional name for the visible divine presence, turning a devotional line into a note on the history of a technical term.

themes: Lord, I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place where thine honour dwelleth.
Gather not my soul with sinners, nor my life with bloody men:
In whose hands is mischief, and their right hand is full of bribes.
But as for me, I will walk in mine integrity: redeem me, and be merciful unto me.
My foot standeth in an even place: in the congregations will I bless the Lord.
